title: Why a 2.9-decisions-a-year investor beat the market: make few decisions, study deeply, wait
summary: Sam profiles an investor who turned ~$10m into ~$50m making about 2.9 buy/sell decisions a year. He distills four habits of successful stock pickers (few decisions, don't agonize over reversible ones, stay in your circle of competence, write decisions down) and applies them to CEOs. The essay is paywalled, so only the opening is available.

principles.text: Motion is not progress: for CEOs and people with leverage, fewer decisions often beat constant activity.
principles.quote: we often correlate motion with good results. But for the average CEO or person with leverage, that isn’t the case.

principles.text: Make few decisions; patient inaction can be the core of a winning strategy.
principles.quote: They make few decisions. “Lethargy bordering on sloth remains the cornerstone of our investment style,” Warren Buffett once said.

principles.text: Sort decisions into irreversible and reversible; don't agonize over two-way doors.
principles.quote: Decisions are split into ones they can’t undo and ones they can easily reverse. Most decisions are two-way doors and don’t deserve agonizing.

principles.text: Know your circle of competence and say no often to things outside it, regardless of whether they look good.
principles.quote: They say “no” often. Not because something is good or bad, but because it’s not within their area of expertise.

principles.text: Write big decisions down with a pre-mortem and your reasoning, then review afterward to judge the reasoning.
principles.quote: Writing pre-mortems (imagine it’s a year later and why the decision blew up) and writing their thought process before the decision. Then they review it after to see if their reasoning was good or bad.

principles.text: Go deep on a few things you can understand, keep detailed notes, and wait for the right opportunity.
principles.quote: I study a few things I feel I can understand, and I study them very deeply. I keep very detailed notes and then just wait for an opportunity.
